find: and Owen uses <dfn class="term" data-def="A form of rhyme in which final consonant sounds match but the vowel sounds differ, creating a jarring, incomplete effect.">para-rhyme</dfn> — near-rhymes like “hymn” and “him” — instead of full rhyme. This creates a sense of things not quite fitting together, echoing the soldier’s broken body.
replace: and Owen rhymes without a fixed scheme, leaving some lines unmatched. He is famous for <dfn class="term" data-def="A form of rhyme in which final consonant sounds match but the vowel sounds differ, creating a jarring, incomplete effect.">para-rhyme</dfn> in his other war poems. Here he rhymes “hymn” with “him” — two words that sound the same but set the boys’ happy voices against the broken man. This creates a sense of things not quite fitting together, echoing the soldier’s broken body.
note: F3: ‘hymn’ and ‘him’ are homophones, so they are not the near-rhyme the lesson's own definition of para-rhyme describes.

value: An irregular rhyme scheme that leaves some lines unmatched.
note: F3: hymn/him is not a near-rhyme.
